extracted.intended_audience: researchers doing meta-research on peer review and authors revising a manuscript for publication
extracted.subtask_description: Designing, analyzing, and reporting a large-scale linguistic analysis of peer review reports (using LIWC and related NLP tools) and preparing the manuscript revisions requested by reviewers. Emphasis on appropriate statistical modelling, dataset description, validity checks, and transparent limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce emphasis on moral bias / remove moral rows from tables
rubrics_metrics.description: Reducing the emphasis on moral bias in the present manuscript will involve deleting the last 10 rows of table 1 (and similarly for tables 2, 3 and 4), and making changes to the text. The title also needs to be changed, but Figure 1 does not need to be changed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delete the specified moral-bias rows across tables, retitle the manuscript to remove moral-bias emphasis, and adjust text accordingly. Keep Figure 1 as is unless further reviewer direction requires it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze LIWC variables with regression / multilevel models
rubrics_metrics.description: The authors should analyze the data they have for word length, analytical thinking, clout, authenticity, emotional tone and morality in general in greater detail through regression analyses and/or multilevel models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Move beyond descriptive/bivariate ANOVAs to regression or multilevel models that account for nested structure and covariates; explore mixed-effects models to better capture within- and between-group variance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider reviewer-profiles and multidimensional classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Build reviewer-profiles based on their characteristics (e.g. reviews with a high degree of clout and negative emotion, and low analytical thinking could be one type). Where is this type found? What characterizes it? Additionally, this would allow the authors to include information about the reviewer, e.g. are they always negative? This might also solve the baseline problem, as this would be a classification issue rather than a measurement issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider classification/clustering approaches to identify multi-variable reviewer types, then examine their distribution across fields/journals and stability across reviews; use this as an alternative or complement to mean comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use mixed methods linear regression with appropriate fixed and random effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Perform mixed methods approach with reviewer recommendation, journal discipline, journal peer review type and reviewer gender as predictors (fixed factors) and different journals, word count and article type as the random factor, which would enable control of variations between journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify predictors and random effects clearly in the model; control for journal-level clustering (random intercepts) and other covariates (word count, article type); report interaction effects and account for potential inflated significance due to large N.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide fuller description of dataset and representativeness / sampling bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Please include a fuller description of your dataset and describe how representative/biased the sampling is by field and type of journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report counts by field, journal, review type, and article type; quantify over-/under-representation (e.g., physical sciences predominance); describe sampling procedure and limitations in Methods and Discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain LIWC measures and calculation; provide sample texts with LIWC scores
rubrics_metrics.description: Please provide more information on what the LIWC measures and how it is calculated? It would be especially helpful if you showed several LIWC scores together with sample texts (preferably from your own database) to illustrate how well it analyses text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe LIWC dictionary approach and that LIWC output is percentage of words in each category; include example passages with corresponding LIWC scores (anonymized if necessary) in an appendix or supplementary file to demonstrate construct validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define baseline effects and provide appropriate comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: What are baseline effects? What kind of changes should we expect? E.g. when arguing that the language is cold and analytical, what is this comparable to?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide benchmarks or comparative corpora (e.g., typical scientific writing or other published referee reports) so readers can interpret absolute LIWC scores; explicitly state expected effect sizes or contextual baselines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for subject-area differences and selection bias across fields/review types
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the analysis allow for the fact that different subject areas will have different LIWC scores? The largest sample of reports comes from the physical sciences, which use single-blind review the most. Reports from this field are also shorter, slightly more analytic and display less Clout and Authenticity. I think your results are picking up this selection bias instead of representing actual differences between the two review processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model field/discipline and peer-review type (single/double blind) and their interactions; report and discuss how field composition affects results; include these factors in multilevel models to reduce confounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Add explicit limitations section covering sample bias and LIWC limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Please add a section on the limitations of your study. For example, there is no discussion of sample bias and representation really. Also, LIWC is full of issues and problems (NLP has come a ways since LIWC arrived on the scene)...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss sampling limitations, field imbalance, reviewer and journal representativeness, and limitations of LIWC (e.g., dictionary approach, psychometric properties). Describe steps taken to mitigate issues and caution about over-interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report LIWC version and psychometric properties (standardized vs raw; Cronbach alphas)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do you use the standardized version of LIWC constructs with high Cronbach alphas, or the raw versions with poor Cronbach alphas?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state which LIWC version and which constructs (standardized/validated scales) were used; report reliability metrics (Cronbach's alpha) where appropriate; if validated constructs were used, document this in Methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate original research content from other content types in analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the analysis distinguish between original research content and other forms of content (eg, editorials, opinion pieces, book reviews etc)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Code article type and include as factor or random effect in models; report counts (e.g., 388,737 original articles and 83,972 other types) and analyze or control for differences by content type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modify tables and figures to present multilevel descriptions and within-group relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Create new tables where we present multilevel description of the review reports based on the interaction effects of the reviewer recommendation, journal discipline, journal peer review type and reviewer gender. Present figures with the within-group relations on standardized scales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace simple mean tables with tables/figures showing multilevel model estimates, interaction effects, and standardized within-group differences; include new graphs for LIWC variables and moral variables in supplementary materials where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use concurrent validity checks with other NLP tools (SentimentR, Stanford CoreNLP)
rubrics_metrics.description: We created the tables for the five LIWC variables ... and two new additional measures (SentimentR ... and Stanford CoreNLP ...), which served as the concurrent validity assessment of the tone variables from the LIWC package.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include results from alternative sentiment / NLP tools to triangulate LIWC findings; report agreement/discrepancies and use them to support validity claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present interaction effects and caution about significance with very large samples
rubrics_metrics.description: We found significant interaction of the reviewer recommendation, journal’s field of research, the type of peer review and reviewer’s gender in each variable assessment, but we understand that this significance could be due to the large sample size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report effect sizes and standardized differences, not just p-values; show interaction plots and within-group relations to convey practical significance; discuss how large N can produce statistically significant but small effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide anonymized examples and supplementary calculation details
rubrics_metrics.description: We now provided the calculation of the different tone variables in the Supplementary file, both for high and low levels of tone. The examples are anonymized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include supplementary material detailing how tone variables were computed and provide anonymized illustrative examples to aid transparency and reader understanding.
